This is working correctly.  sapply() is returning a named vector, and <NA> is the name of the single element.  Notice that the sapply() in the working block returns a named list, and compare what happens with `sapply(c(zoo = NA_character_), is.na <http://is.na>)`.

I don’t understand why sapply() is returning a named vector in this particular case.  But named vectors will behave like unnamed vectors, except that you have some additional ways of accessing their values.  So you should be able to safely assign this to val and proceed with the rest of your script.

If for some reason you really want to get rid of the names, use `names(val) <- NULL` after the sapply().

Cheers,
Dan

messages.body_plain:
If you know the start and end time of sample set, you should create a date vector  using "seq" for the given resolution. Then make an empty data frame or matrix with first column as date vector and another one is NaN. Then look the specific date or time value in your sample and fill the cells in the second column. Then you use the modified set from the data matrix. I have  made a function to fill the set below.  I hope this helps you. If you have any questions, please let me know.

fillSet <- function(rawData){
  dateVec = as.character(rawData$TIMESTAMP)
  dateVec = as.POSIXct(dateVec, tz = 'UTC', format='%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')
  rawData$TIMESTAMP = dateVec
  colNames <-colnames(rawData)
  date1 = dateVec[1] # Starting date or time
  date2 = dateVec[length(dateVec)] # End date or time
  vecDATE = seq(date1, date2, by=1800, tz = Sys.timezone())
  newRawData = data.frame(matrix(NaN, nrow = length(vecDATE), ncol = ncol(rawData)))
  colnames(newRawData)<-colNames
  newRawData[colNames[1]] = vecDATE
  for(i in 1:nrow(rawData)){
    print(paste('Filling line', i))
    idfind = which(vecDATE==rawData[i, colNames[1]])[1]

    newRawData[idfind, 1] = rawData[i, 1]
    for(j in 2:ncol(rawData)){
      newRawData[idfind, j] = as.numeric(as.character(rawData[i,  j]))
    }

  }
  return(newRawData)
}

Usage
## dataMatrix with one column time of observation and another one could be variable.
dataMatrix.Filled = fillSet(dataMatrix)
## Extract Samples from this matrix
sampleData = dataMatrix.Fille[, c(firstColumn,  VariableName)]
calculate correlation for each lag.
Note that there may be many NaN, so you need to deal with nan Values.
If you find this routine find useful and need correction and clarification let me know.

Good luck,
Mahesh

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vadim

Are you looking at auto-correlation over time or space? acf() is for time, but it seems you are thinking of space (i.e.: "irregularly spaced sampling sites")?

If it is over time, you should just replace missing values with NA, then use na.action = na.pass in acf(). A simple way to use cast missing obs into explicit NA is with tidyr::complete(), like:

library(tidyverse)
data_frame(index_x = index_x,
           x = x_miss) %>%
  complete(index_x = 1:N)

you can easily create a sequence of dates, from start to end with something like: as.Date(as.Date("2015-01-01") :  as.Date("2015-10-01"))

Full example:

library(zoo)
#>
#> Attaching package: 'zoo'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#>
#>     as.Date, as.Date.numeric

N <-  5000
x <- arima.sim(model = list(ma = c(0.2, 0.9)), n = N)
set.seed(123)
index_x <-  sort(sample(1:N, size = N/5, replace = FALSE))
x_miss <-  x[index_x]

acf(x[1:(N/5)])

#' ![](reprex_reprex_files/figure-markdown_strict/reprex-body-1.png)

acf(x_miss)

#' ![](reprex_reprex_files/figure-markdown_strict/reprex-body-2.png)

## fill x
library(tidyverse)
df <- data_frame(index_x = index_x,
                 x = x_miss)

df_clean <-  df %>%
  complete(index_x = 1:N)

df_clean
#> # A tibble: 5,000 x 2
#>    index_x       x
#>      <int>   <dbl>
#>  1       1  NA
#>  2       2  NA
#>  3       3  -0.471
#>  4       4  -0.710
#>  5       5  NA
#>  6       6  -0.604
#>  7       7  NA
#>  8       8  NA
#>  9       9  NA
#> 10      10  NA
#> # ... with 4,990 more rows

acf(df_clean$x, na.action = na.pass)

#' ![](reprex_reprex_files/figure-markdown_strict/reprex-body-3.png)

If I'm understanding correctly, it sounds like you want Rich's first suggestion:

library(dplyr)

d %>%

  group_by(Location, Meter, Texture) %>%
  summarise(avg_n <- mean(N2O))

The difference is only in the variables you're grouping by. Think of it this way: Vince's method will be returning a mean N2O for every unique combination of Location, Meter, Texture, and Time in the dataset (115 unique combos in your sample data); Rich's first suggestion will be returning a mean N2O value for every unique combination of Location, Meter, and Texture in the dataset (32 unique combos in your sample data). So if you want to average across times, I think you want Rich's code.

You may also be running into the namespace issues Vince just mentioned, since you shouldn't be getting only one row/value...
